questions.solution:
First, note [latex]\text{bar}(n)[/latex] repeatedly integer-halves [latex]n[/latex] until reaching [latex]1[/latex], counting the number of halvings — this is exactly [latex]\lfloor\log_2 n\rfloor[/latex].

[latex]\text{foo}(n)=1+\text{foo}(\text{bar}(n))[/latex] for [latex]n>1[/latex], and [latex]\text{foo}(1)=1[/latex]. So [latex]\text{foo}(n)[/latex] counts [latex]1[/latex] plus the number of times we must apply [latex]\text{bar}[/latex] (i.e. take [latex]\lfloor\log_2\cdot\rfloor[/latex]) starting from [latex]n[/latex] to eventually reach [latex]1[/latex].

Build up the smallest [latex]n[/latex] achieving each target value of [latex]\text{foo}[/latex]:
- [latex]\text{foo}(n)=1[/latex]: smallest [latex]n=1[/latex].
- [latex]\text{foo}(n)=2[/latex]: need [latex]\text{bar}(n)=1[/latex], i.e. [latex]\lfloor\log_2 n\rfloor=1[/latex]: smallest [latex]n=2[/latex].
- [latex]\text{foo}(n)=3[/latex]: need [latex]\text{bar}(n)=2[/latex]: smallest [latex]n=2^2=4[/latex].
- [latex]\text{foo}(n)=4[/latex]: need [latex]\text{bar}(n)=4[/latex]: smallest [latex]n=2^4=16[/latex].
- [latex]\text{foo}(n)=5[/latex]: need [latex]\text{bar}(n)=16[/latex]: smallest [latex]n=2^{16}=65536[/latex].

Answer: 65536

questions.text:
The following sequence corresponds to the preorder traversal of a binary search tree [latex]T[/latex] :

[latex] 50,25,13,40,30,47,75,60,70,80,77 [/latex]

The position of the element [latex]60[/latex] in the postorder traversal of [latex]T[/latex] is ________ . (answer in integer)
Note: The position begins with [latex]1[/latex].
questions.solution:
Reconstruct the BST from the preorder [latex]50,25,13,40,30,47,75,60,70,80,77[/latex] (each root's left subtree holds smaller values, right subtree holds larger values, read off in preorder root-first fashion):

[latex]50[/latex] is the root. Left subtree (values [latex]<50[/latex]): [latex]25,13,40,30,47[/latex]; right subtree (values [latex]>50[/latex]): [latex]75,60,70,80,77[/latex].
Left subtree: root [latex]25[/latex], left child [latex]13[/latex] (leaf), right subtree [latex]40,30,47[/latex] → root [latex]40[/latex], left [latex]30[/latex], right [latex]47[/latex].
Right subtree: root [latex]75[/latex], left subtree [latex]60,70[/latex] → root [latex]60[/latex] with right child [latex]70[/latex] (no left); right subtree [latex]80,77[/latex] → root [latex]80[/latex] with left child [latex]77[/latex] (no right).

Postorder (left, right, root) of the whole tree:
From the [latex]25[/latex]-subtree: [latex]13,\ 30,47,40,\ 25[/latex]
From the [latex]75[/latex]-subtree: [latex]70,60,\ 77,80,\ 75[/latex]
Then the root [latex]50[/latex].

Full postorder: [latex]13,\,30,\,47,\,40,\,25,\,70,\,60,\,77,\,80,\,75,\,50[/latex]

Counting positions (starting at [latex]1[/latex]): [latex]60[/latex] is the [latex]7[/latex]th element.

Answer: 7

Click here for detail solution

Trace the loop, remembering that after [latex]\text{fork()}[/latex], the child gets return value [latex]0[/latex] (executes [latex]\text{continue}[/latex], moving to the next loop iteration), while the parent gets a nonzero value (executes [latex]\text{break}[/latex], immediately leaving the loop).

- [latex]i=0[/latex]: original process forks → parent breaks immediately (1 process reaches printf with [latex]i=0[/latex]); the child continues the loop.
- [latex]i=1[/latex] (in that child): it forks again → this process (now acting as parent of its own fork) breaks (2nd process reaches printf); its own child continues.
- [latex]i=2[/latex] (in that grandchild): forks again → this one breaks (3rd process reaches printf); its child continues.
- [latex]i=3[/latex] (in the great-grandchild): loop condition [latex]i<3[/latex] fails, so the loop ends naturally without another fork (4th process reaches printf).

So exactly [latex]4[/latex] distinct processes each execute the [latex]\text{printf}[/latex] statement exactly once.

Answer: 4

questions.text: Consider a CPU that has to execute two types of processes. The first type, Actuators (A), requires a CPU burst of [latex]6[/latex] seconds. The second type, Controllers (C), requires a CPU burst of [latex]8[/latex] seconds. A new process of type A arrives at time [latex]t=10[/latex], [latex]20, 30, 40[/latex], and [latex]50[/latex] (in seconds). Similarly, a new process of type C arrives at time [latex]t=[/latex] [latex]11, 22, 33, 44[/latex], and [latex]55[/latex] (in seconds). The CPU scheduling policy is First Come First Serve (FCFS). The first process of type A starts running at [latex]t=10[/latex] seconds. The average waiting time (in seconds) for the [latex]10[/latex] processes is ________. (rounded off to one decimal place)
questions.solution:
List all [latex]10[/latex] arrivals in chronological order and simulate FCFS execution (CPU serves strictly in arrival order, non-preemptive):

[latex]\begin{array}{c|c|c|c|c|c}\text{Proc}&\text{Arrival}&\text{Burst}&\text{Start}&\text{Finish}&\text{Waiting}\\\hline A&10&6&10&16&0\\C&11&8&16&24&5\\A&20&6&24&30&4\\C&22&8&30&38&8\\A&30&6&38&44&8\\C&33&8&44&52&11\\A&40&6&52&58&12\\C&44&8&58&66&14\\A&50&6&66&72&16\\C&55&8&72&80&17\end{array}[/latex]

Sum of waiting times [latex]=0+5+4+8+8+11+12+14+16+17=95[/latex].

Average waiting time [latex]=\dfrac{95}{10}=9.5[/latex] seconds.

Answer: 9.5

questions.text: Consider a relational database schema with a relation [latex]R(A, B, C, D)[/latex]. If [latex]\{A, B\}[/latex] and [latex]\{A, C\}[/latex] are the only two candidate keys of the relation [latex]R[/latex], then the number of superkeys of relation [latex]R[/latex] is ________. (answer in integer)
questions.solution:
A superkey is any subset of attributes that contains at least one candidate key as a subset. Here the [latex]4[/latex] attributes are [latex]\{A,B,C,D\}[/latex] and the candidate keys are [latex]\{A,B\}[/latex] and [latex]\{A,C\}[/latex].

Count subsets of [latex]\{A,B,C,D\}[/latex] containing [latex]\{A,B\}[/latex]: freely choose the remaining [latex]\{C,D\}[/latex] → [latex]2^2=4[/latex] subsets.
Count subsets containing [latex]\{A,C\}[/latex]: freely choose the remaining [latex]\{B,D\}[/latex] → [latex]2^2=4[/latex] subsets.
Subsets counted twice are those containing both [latex]\{A,B\}[/latex] and [latex]\{A,C\}[/latex], i.e. containing [latex]\{A,B,C\}[/latex]: freely choose remaining [latex]\{D\}[/latex] → [latex]2^1=2[/latex] subsets.

By inclusion-exclusion, total superkeys [latex]=4+4-2=6[/latex].

Answer: 6
